endorsements.title: CHAI AI governance frameworks (playbooks)
endorsements.quote: Identify and document the tools and resources available and needed to implement and maintain an AI inventory registry to track internal and third party solutions.

endorsements.title: CHAI Responsible AI Guide (Assurance Standards Guide)
endorsements.quote: Decide whether the AI solution will be reported within a registry, inventory, or centralized data platform, and identify whether the implementing organization has an established quality management system with which AI solution development must comply.

endorsements.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework: Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1)
endorsements.issuer: National Institute of Standards and Technology

endorsements.title: The EU AI Act: implications and compliance guidance for healthcare facilities
endorsements.quote: Once governance structures are established, the next critical task is to conduct a thorough inventory and classification of all AI systems in use.

endorsements.title: The VIBE-HI framework: a conceptual model for evaluating vibe coding appropriateness, quality, and safety in health informatics
endorsements.quote: Third, an accountability register recording, for each deployed tool, its tier, clinical purpose, owner, and review date—the minimum needed to satisfy an audit.

commentary.bottom_line: Five sources, three frameworks and two commentaries, endorse a centralized AI inventory with named owners, but no supplied study tests whether keeping one reduces untracked AI use or patient harm. The recommendation currently rests on expert consensus and regulatory expectation rather than measured outcomes.

perspectives.view: No study tests the practice, and no study documents how often untracked AI systems operate in health systems. Certainty cannot be rated above no direct evidence. The five endorsements agree on direction, but agreement among frameworks and commentaries does not substitute for comparative data on outcomes.

A commentary on the EU AI Act describes inventory and classification of all AI systems in use as a step that follows governance setup, and NIST AI 600-1 asks organizations to define human oversight roles. For systems subject to these regimes, an inventory may serve as a compliance record whatever its measured effect on safety.

The CHAI playbook asks organizations to identify the tools and resources needed to build and maintain a registry, which implies ongoing staffing and software costs. No supplied study reports those costs, the effort needed to keep an inventory current, or how completeness is verified at scale.

The VIBE-HI commentary proposes recording tier, clinical purpose, owner, and review date for each tool as the minimum for audit. The logic is that a system nobody knows about cannot be monitored, but no supplied study shows that an inventory catches failures before they reach patients.

commentary.research_gap: Studies are needed that measure how many AI systems in a health system go unrecorded before and after an inventory is established, whether named ownership shortens the time to detect and correct AI malfunctions, and what staffing and tooling it takes to keep an inventory complete and current.
commentary.underserved_note: No study tested the practice, so no evidence exists on whether an inventory performs differently in Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy settings. Safety-net systems may have fewer resources for inventory tooling, and that possibility remains untested.
